sourceTextMethod: Original historically identified editions/translated historical texts accessible as online transcriptions or OCR, plus Latin Summa; no independent printed-page visual proof.
basis: Existing 32-case comparison ledger and user-owned 2026-10-15 Passage Deduplication & Source Handoff.
originalEditionWarnings: Guéranger text identifies an 1885 second edition compiled from conference notes; foreword expressly warns original note-taking/copying may be imperfect. Treat attribution as 'Guéranger conference notes, 1885 ed.', not a verbatim authorial manuscript.

The St Alphonsus online English witness is the Eugene Grimm-edited 1887 Centenary Edition vol VI. Its editor's notice identifies an earlier *unnamed* French author, with tentative discussion of Condren/Quesnel. This CANNOT be Dom Prosper Guéranger (1805–1875), who postdates St Alphonsus (1696–1787). Do not equate that unnamed French source with Guéranger or register an unsupported donor identity.
Gihr's online 1902 edition is an English translation from German; printed page labels in OCR are identifiable but the facsimile page image is not independently checked in this pass.
Aquinas ST III q.83 a.4 ad 7–9 is directly checkable in a Latin/English scholarly transcription; an online transcription does not establish medieval manuscript critical-text collation.
Three scriptural-sacrificial types and mystical allegories must remain separate from the literal statements of Genesis 4, 14, 22 and the 1962 rubric.
Attribution/synthesis approval is not text-reproduction permission. Shared Reference owns work/edition/witness, rights and stable link qualification.

sixPairTranscriptionCollations.author: St Alphonsus
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.edition: 1887 English Centenary Edition, vol. VI, edited by Eugene Grimm
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.locator: Short Explanation of the Prayers of Mass, Supplices te rogamus; printed pp.56–57
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.result: One received passage summarizes an angel presiding at Mass, an earlier unidentified French author's Christological reading, and a preference for the ministering angel presenting prayer. The two legacy summaries refer to this same paragraph, but retain both IDs.

sixPairTranscriptionCollations.author: Dom Prosper Guéranger (conference notes)
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.edition: 1885 second edition, Imprimerie Saint-Pierre, Solesmes; editorially compiled conference notes
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.locator: MEMENTO DES VIVANTS, et omnium circumstantium
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.result: The celebrant commends the faithful physically present and stresses their faith and devotion. Both claim summaries return to the same adjacent sentences; one compact study claim with two provenance IDs.

sixPairTranscriptionCollations.author: Dom Prosper Guéranger (conference notes)
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.edition: 1885 second edition, Imprimerie Saint-Pierre, Solesmes; editorially compiled conference notes
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.result: The word rationabilem is explained by reference to a truly spiritual oblation and Romans 12:1. Other details address the neighbouring crosses and transformation; synthesize the shared word meaning without losing separate sign-cue commentary.

sixPairTranscriptionCollations.author: Nicholas Gihr
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.edition: 1902 English translation of sixth German edition (German original not collated)
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.locator: The Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, §61, printed p.659, Abel
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.result: Both describe Abel's faithful offering and innocent death prefiguring Christ. One text also speculates that fire may have consumed Abel's offering; Genesis does not establish this.

sixPairTranscriptionCollations.author: Nicholas Gihr
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.edition: 1902 English translation of sixth German edition (German original not collated)
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.locator: The Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, §61, printed p.659, Abraham
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.result: Both summarize Abraham's faith and willingness to offer Isaac; Gihr explicitly makes clear Isaac's blood was not shed. Keep figurative language separate from the historical Genesis event.

sixPairTranscriptionCollations.author: Nicholas Gihr
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.edition: 1902 English translation of sixth German edition (German original not collated)
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.locator: The Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, §61, printed pp.660 and earlier broader Melchisedech chapters
sixPairTranscriptionCollations.result: Both place bread-and-wine offering in Eucharistic sacrificial typology, but the former also discusses Christian priesthood. Genesis 14:18 describes the bread and wine without explicitly describing a sacrificial rite.

sourceWitnesses.finding: Identifies the angel Christologically as Christ, the one sent by the Father.

sourceWitnesses.work: Aquinas ST III q.83 a.4 ad 9
sourceWitnesses.finding: Explicit two alternatives: ministering angel presenting prayers; Christ himself as Angel of Great Counsel.
Repeats both readings; prefers angelic prayer presentation; 'our French author' cannot be Guéranger, a later writer.
Comparison concerns ancient offerers' devotion, not parity of sacrificial value; three distinct typologies.

sourceWitnesses.work: Aquinas ST III q.83 a.4 ad 8
sourceWitnesses.finding: Ancient offerings pleasing because of offerers' devotion, not because Eucharist lacked value.
No parity between Christ's sacrifice and those of Abel/Abraham/Melchisedech.
Explains adscriptam/ratam/rationabilem with Romans 12:1, and distinguishes the crosses.
Gives lexical gloss for five adjectives and notes Aquinas's qualification.

sourceWitnesses.work: Aquinas ST III q.83 a.4 ad 7 Latin
sourceWitnesses.finding: Reading concerns sanctifying fruit for us; distinct from strict dictionary definition or efficacy of signs.
Draws an Old Law sacrifice imposition-of-hands analogy.
Offers spiritual significance of offering oneself with the victim and recalls Old Law hand placement.
Compares Luke and Matthew, Hebrews' eternal covenant, and traditio for Mysterium fidei; pro multis distinction treated by author.
One complete Latin received formula on one source cue; multiple word-level explanation points.
